subject: geography
title: The Demographic Transition Model
welcome_lead: Trace the five stages of demographic transition, from high-stationary populations to post-industrial decline.
meta_desc: IBDP Geography Adventure: the Demographic Transition Model and its application to world populations.
final_note: You have followed birth and death rates through history. The DTM is a powerful — if simplified — lens on population change.

concepts.def: Five-stage model describing the shift from high birth and death rates to low rates as countries develop.
Number of live births per 1,000 population per year.
Number of deaths per 1,000 population per year.
Difference between CBR and CDR, expressed as a percentage.
Average number of children born to a woman over her lifetime; replacement level ~2.1.
Post-industrial stage in which birth rates fall below death rates and populations decline.

walkthroughs.body_html: Stage 1 (high stationary) shows high CBR and CDR (>35‰) and low growth — characteristic of hunter-gatherer or pre-modern societies. Stage 2 (early expanding) features rapidly falling death rates due to improved sanitation, vaccination and food supply while births remain high, producing high natural increase — observed in many Sub-Saharan African countries today.

Stage 3 (late expanding) features falling birth rates linked to urbanisation, female education and contraception — visible in India, Indonesia and parts of Latin America. Stage 4 (low stationary) shows low CBR and CDR, slow growth and ageing populations — most of Europe, North America and East Asia.

Stage 5 (declining) sees CBR below CDR, producing natural decrease — Japan, Italy, Germany and South Korea face shrinking working-age populations, pension pressures and policy responses including pro-natalism and immigration. Global population reached approximately 8 billion in November 2022.
